metadata.note: South Texas - the largest hole the map had. Corpus Christi, Laredo and Brownsville had no passenger rail drawn in any year, and Austin’s nearest drawn line was 66 km away, even though all four were served for decades. This layer draws the Missouri Pacific system that served them: the International-Great Northern from Taylor through Austin and San Antonio to Laredo (1876-1881), the San Antonio, Uvalde and Gulf - the "Sausage" - from San Antonio to Corpus Christi (1912-14), and the St. Louis, Brownsville and Mexico - the "Brownie" - from Robstown into the Lower Rio Grande Valley (1904); plus the independent Texas Mexican Railway from Corpus Christi to Laredo (1881). Two of the three Missouri Pacific predecessors are split at their purchase dates per the map’s one-company-one-colour rule: the SAU&G in its own colour to December 1925 and the Brownie to the same date, with Missouri Pacific blue (#0057B8) after. The I-GN is drawn in Missouri Pacific blue throughout, since Jay Gould took control in December 1880, four years into its life, and it ran as a Missouri Pacific property from then until the outright merger of March 1 1956. The trains: the Sunshine Special from 1915, the Texas Eagle from August 1948 (with sections for Austin, San Antonio and Laredo) and the Valley Eagle from October 1948 (Houston - Brownsville, 371 miles, with a Corpus Christi section). The Valley Eagle’s last run was in 1962; the Eagle between Laredo and Texarkana was cancelled on September 21 1970, the last Missouri Pacific passenger train in Texas.

Node-id graph, Dijkstra between terminal stations, Douglas-Peucker at 15 m.
not_yet_sourced: When the Texas Mexican Railway’s own regular passenger service ended is not sourced anywhere consulted - TSHA, Wikipedia and american-rails all skip it. The Corpus Christi - Laredo feature is therefore drawn 1881-1902 and again 1986-89 with a deliberate hole between, rather than a guessed end year. Resolving this needs an Official Guide or a Texas Mexican timetable.

A nameless night train is reported to have continued on the Corpus Christi route into 1965 or 1966 after the Valley Eagle was dropped in 1962. The report is too loose to draw (it does not say which segment), so both Corpus Christi features end in 1962 - an under-draw of up to four years.

The Valley Eagle’s Houston - Robstown leg (the St. Louis, Brownsville and Mexico line of December 31 1907, via Bay City and Victoria) is not drawn: the OSM Brownsville and Angleton subdivision relations do not connect through to Houston, so the Valley line currently ends at Robstown.
The San Antonio and Aransas Pass route from San Antonio to Corpus Christi via Kenedy and Beeville - a separate railroad from the SAU&G line drawn here - is not drawn at all.
No Missouri Pacific timetable was consulted for this layer, so every avg_speed_kmh on the I-GN features and every pre-1948 headway_min in the file is an estimate.
metadata.passenger_only_rule: Features end at the end of passenger service: 1962 in the Valley and at Corpus Christi, 1970 on the Austin - San Antonio - Laredo main line. Union Pacific and CPKC still run freight over all of it. Amtrak’s Texas Eagle returned to the San Antonio - Austin - Taylor segment and is drawn in data/amtrak.geojson, not here.

segments.note: Texas Eagle era: the Missouri Pacific’s streamliner debuted in mid-August 1948 and ran St. Louis and Memphis to Texas, with sections that split for Austin, San Antonio and Laredo. Missouri Pacific passenger service over this line ended on September 21 1970, when the Texas Railroad Commission granted the railroad’s request to cancel the Eagle between Laredo and Texarkana effective immediately - the two trains already running became the last. Amtrak did not take the route over in 1971; it returned to Austin and San Antonio later and is drawn separately in data/amtrak.geojson.
sources: Segment-level: the mid-August 1948 Texas Eagle debut is from american-rails.com and the Wikipedia Texas Eagle (MP train) article; the September 21 1970 Texas Railroad Commission cancellation is from arkansasrailroadhistory.com.

segments.note: The "Sausage" - the nickname came from the initials SAU&G - built south from San Antonio through Pleasanton to Fowlerton, 78 miles opened November 19 1912, and then the 117-mile Pleasanton Junction to Corpus Christi line in stages between January 30 1913 and February 28 1914. This feature is drawn from 1914, when the whole route it covers was open. The railroad was independent until the New Orleans, Texas and Mexico bought it for the Missouri Pacific on December 1 1925, where this feature ends and the Missouri Pacific-coloured one begins. headway_min is an unsourced estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the November 19 1912 San Antonio - Fowlerton opening, the January 30 1913 - February 28 1914 Pleasanton Junction - Corpus Christi stages, the "Sausage" nickname and the December 1 1925 purchase are all from the TSHA SAU&G handbook entry, which also records passenger earnings of $247,000 in 1916. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates.

segments.note: The "Brownie", chartered June 6 1903 as part of Benjamin Yoakum’s Chicago-to-Mexico-City scheme: the first segment of track, Robstown to Brownsville, was completed on July 4 1904 and opened the Lower Rio Grande Valley to the rest of the country. Its Robstown - Houston line followed on December 31 1907. The securities passed to the Gulf Coast Lines in 1916 and the Missouri Pacific bought the property in December 1924, taking effective control from 1925. headway_min is an unsourced estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the June 6 1903 charter, the July 4 1904 Robstown - Brownsville completion, the December 31 1907 Houston line, the Gulf Coast Lines era and the December 1924 Missouri Pacific purchase are all from the Wikipedia St. Louis, Brownsville and Mexico article. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates.

properties.speed_source: From the Tex-Mex Express: 157 miles Corpus Christi - Laredo in about 4.5 hours = 35 mph = 56 km/h. That is the 1986-89 excursion-era schedule, the only one found; nineteenth-century running was slower.

segments.note: Three-foot narrow gauge, built west from Corpus Christi to Rancho Banquete between 1875 and 1877 and on to San Diego, Texas by 1879; the Texas Mexican Railway charter of 1881 carried it the remaining 110 miles to Laredo, completed in September 1881. This feature is drawn from 1881, when the whole Corpus Christi - Laredo route it covers was open, and stops in 1902 at the standard-gauging - NOT because service ended then. The end of the railroad’s regular passenger service could not be sourced, so the years between are left undrawn rather than guessed; see the layer’s not_yet_sourced field. headway_min is an unsourced estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the 1875-79 narrow-gauge construction, the September 1881 completion to Laredo and the July 17 1902 standard-gauging are from the TSHA Texas Mexican Railway entry and the Wikipedia article. The 1902 end year is a deliberate under-draw, not a sourced discontinuance. headway_min is an estimate.

segments.note: The Tex-Mex Express, January 31 1986 to June 18 1989: one round trip on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays through the spring and summer, 157 miles Corpus Christi - Robstown - Alice - Hebbronville - Laredo in about four and a half hours. headway_min 4320 reflects a train that ran three days a week, not daily.
sources: Segment-level: the January 31 1986 - June 18 1989 dates, the weekend-only seasonal pattern, the 157-mile route, the intermediate stops and the 4.5-hour running time are from the Wikipedia Texas Mexican Railway article.
